etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English blot (“blot, spot, stain, blemish”). Perhaps from Old Norse *blettr (“blot, stain”) (only attested in documents from after Old Norse transitioned to Icelandic blettur), or from Old French bloche (“clod of earth”).

definitions.definition: A blemish, spot or stain made by a coloured substance.

quote.citation: 1595 December 9 (first known performance), William Shakespeare, “The life and death of King Richard the Second”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies: Published According to the True Originall Copies (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene i], page 28, column 2:
quote.text: England bound in with the triumphant ſea, / Whoſe rocky ſhore beates backe the enuious ſiedge / Of watery Neptune, is now bound in with ſhame, / With Inky blottes, and rotten Parchment bonds.

quote.citation: 1711 [December?] (date written), Jonathan Swift, “An Excellent New Song. Being the Intended Speech of a Famous Orator against Peace [i.e., Daniel Finch, 2nd Earl of Nottingham].”, in Thomas Sheridan, John Nichols, editors, The Works of the Rev. Jonathan Swift, […], new edition, volume VII, London:  […]  J[oseph] Johnson, […], published 1801, →OCLC, page 72:
quote.text: When I and some others subscribed our names / To a plot for expelling my master king James [James II of England]; / I withdrew my subscription by help of a blot, / And so might discover or gain by the plot:  […]

quote.citation: 1849 May – 1850 November, Charles Dickens, “Chapter XVII. Somebody Turns Up.”, in The Personal History of David Copperfield, London: Bradbury & Evans, […], published 1850, →OCLC, page 176:
quote.text: Her utmost powers of expression (which were certainly not great in ink) were exhausted in the attempt to write what she felt on the subject of my journey. Four sides of incoherent and interjectional beginnings of sentences, that had no end, except blots, were inadequate to afford her any relief. But the blots were more expressive to me than the best composition; for they showed me that Peggotty had been crying all over the paper, and what could I have desired more?

quote.citation: 1918, Siegfried Sassoon, “The Death-Bed”, in The Old Huntsman and Other Poems‎[1], London: Heinemann, page 95:
quote.text: […]  He was blind; he could not see the starsGlinting among the wraiths of wandering cloud;Queer blots of colour, purple, scarlet, green,Flickered and faded in his drowning eyes.

definitions.definition: (by extension) A stain on someone's reputation or character; a disgrace.

quote.citation: 1595 December 9 (first known performance), William Shakespeare, “The life and death of King Richard the Second”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies: Published According to the True Originall Copies (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene iii], page 43, column 1:
quote.text: Thy ouerflow of good, conuerts to bad, / And thy abundant goodneſſe ſhall excuſe / This deadly blot, in thy digreſſing ſonne.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Proverbs 9:7, column 2:
quote.text: He that reproueth a ſcorner, getteth to himſelfe ſhame: and he that rebuketh a wicked man, getteth himſelfe a blot.

quote.citation: 1785, William Cowper, “Book II. The Time-piece.”, in The Task, a Poem, […], London:  […]  J[oseph] Johnson;  […], →OCLC, page 46:
quote.text: Thus man devotes his brother, and deſtroys; / And worſe than all, and moſt to be deplored / As human nature’s broadeſt, fouleſt blot, / Chains him, and taſks him, and exacts his ſweat / With ſtripes, that mercy with a bleeding heart / Weeps when ſhe ſees inflicted on a beaſt.

quote.citation: 1960 February, “The dieselised St. Pancras suburban service”, in Trains Illustrated, page 95:
quote.text: The only blot on this service is that of its Kentish Town connections, which throughout the day in many cases just miss the St. Pancras-Luton stopping trains.

definitions.definition: (biochemistry) A method of transferring proteins, DNA or RNA, onto a carrier.
(transitive) To cause a blot (on something) by spilling a coloured substance.
(intransitive) To soak up or absorb liquid.
(transitive) To dry (writing, etc.) with blotting paper.
(transitive) To spot, stain, or bespatter, as with ink.

quote.citation: 1566, George Gascoigne, Dan Bartholmew of Bath:
quote.text: The briefe was writte and blotted all with gore, […]

definitions.definition: (transitive) To impair; to damage; to mar; to soil.

quote.citation: c. 1590–1592 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Taming of the Shrew”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene ii], page 229, column 1:
quote.text: It blots thy beautie, as froſts doe bite the Meads, […]

definitions.definition: (transitive) To stain with infamy; to disgrace.

quote.text: Blot not thy Innocence with guiltleſs Blood.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To obliterate, as writing with ink; to cancel; to efface; generally with out.

quote.citation: 1681, John Dryden, The Spanish Fryar: Or, the Double Discovery. […], London:  […]  Richard Tonson and Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC, Act V, page 82:
quote.text: One act like this blots out a thouſand Crimes.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To obscure; to eclipse; to shadow.

quote.text: He ſung how Earth blots the Moons gilded Wane, […]

definitions.definition: (transitive, MLE) To sell illegal drugs, to deal, to push.

quote.text: I'm walking down the street, past the coppers on the beat. Past the shotters blottin' weed, clear for everyone to see.
